## Limit profile {#sec-recipe-aggregate-limit-profile}

You have the shape every pricing actuary already has: a table of premium by limit band, each band with its own expected loss ratio. You want one aggregate distribution for the whole book, with the bands correctly weighted -- not three separate models you then have to add up by hand.

```{python}
a = build('''agg LimitProfile
  [10000 20000 5000] premium at [0.8 0.7 0.5] lr
  [1000 2000 5000] xs 0
  sev lognorm 50 cv 1.5
  poisson''')
qd(a.summary_df)
```

The three vectors line up positionally: 10000 of premium at an 80% loss ratio written at a 1000 limit, 20000 at 70% at a 2000 limit, 5000 at 50% at a 5000 limit. One severity curve is written across all three bands, and the *limit* is what differs -- so the severity is the same lognormal capped at three different points.

The claim count is an **output**, not an input. `aggregate` knows the expected loss in each band (premium x loss ratio) and the expected severity in that band (the lognormal limited at that band's limit), so it derives the implied count per band and adds them. That is the whole point of the exposure clause: you give it what you actually have -- premium and a loss ratio -- and it solves for the count rather than making you do it.

Read `a.n` back to see the implied total count, and `a.sev_m` for the exposure-weighted average severity across the bands.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The check"}

```{python}
# the aggregate mean IS the premium-weighted expected loss, exactly:
# 10000x0.8 + 20000x0.7 + 5000x0.5 = 24500
assert abs(a.actual_m - 24500.0) < 1e-9
# and the FFT estimate agrees to grid accuracy
assert abs(a.est_m / a.actual_m - 1) < 1e-6
# E[A] = E[N] x E[X] still holds across the blended profile
assert abs(a.n * a.sev_m - a.actual_m) < 1e-6
```

:::

## Three dice: an exact discrete aggregate {#sec-recipe-aggregate-three-dice}

You want to see what `aggregate` computes on something you can check in your head. Three dice: a fixed frequency of 3, a severity uniform on 1..6.

```{python}
a = build('''agg ThreeDice
  dfreq [3]
  dsev [1 2 3 4 5 6]''')
qd(a.summary_df)
```

Everything here is discrete and lands exactly on the grid, so this is the one case where the FFT is not an approximation at all -- the aggregate PMF is the exact three-fold convolution of the die. That is why it is the first recipe: it separates "is the method right" from "is the discretization fine", which every later recipe has to hold apart.

`dfreq [3]` is an explicit outcome list with a single outcome, so N = 3 with probability one. `dsev [1:6]` is the inclusive range 1, 2, ..., 6 with equal weights.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The check"}

```{python}
# E[A] = 3 x 3.5 = 10.5, and the estimate is EXACT, not merely close
assert abs(a.actual_m - 10.5) < 1e-12
assert abs(a.est_m - 10.5) < 1e-9
# support runs 3..18; each extreme has probability (1/6)^3
assert abs(a.density_df.loc[3, 'p_total'] - (1 / 6) ** 3) < 1e-12
assert abs(a.density_df.loc[18, 'p_total'] - (1 / 6) ** 3) < 1e-12
```

:::
